POST in the same state is still refused `E_LOCKED`. The audit row's
`principal` is `notify:<id>`, carries the key count and no key, and names
no person.

**F.238 (v0.84).** The dense layer is built as a job. `POST
/v1/admin/canopy` answers 202 with a job for a build and for `{refresh:
true}`; the job reports progress, is cancellable, and is refused
`E_LOCKED` naming the running job while an ingest runs on that forest — and
an ingest POST is refused the same way while a build runs. A cancelled
build leaves the forest with the index it had: `canopy_status` — `model`,
`nodes`, `stale` — is byte-identical to before the build started, and a
`locate` behaves exactly as it did. **Negative control:** `GET
/v1/admin/canopy` is unchanged, synchronous, takes no job and touches no
lock; and F.42 passes unmodified.

### J.12 Out of scope for Part J

Engine changes of any kind (contracts, budgets, ranking); per-node ACLs
finer than the branch prefix; row-level filtering inside datasets beyond
the table allow-list; multi-writer forests (the single-writer lock stands);
billing and metering beyond per-token quotas.

*Documented boundary (informative):* scoping is per node, and node bodies
are author-written prose. A body that names an out-of-scope node discloses
that id to anyone who may read the body the remedy is to keep such
references in the same scope, not to redact prose, which would corrupt the
content the forest exists to serve.

## Part K The Gauntlet (query-conditioned frontier, v0.21)

### K.0 Why it is not the entry search

Part C's `locate` answers *where do I start*. Parts C.3–C.5 answer *where
do I go next*, and they answer it without knowing what the forager is
looking for: `look` sorts edges by heat, `scan` sorts children by degree,
`move` does not sort. Heat is the memory of past hunts and degree is the
shape of the graph; neither is about **this** question.

The Gauntlet is the instrument that closes that gap a query-conditioned
ordering of the *frontier*, i.e. the set of nodes reachable in one step
from where the forager stands. In information-foraging terms it makes
proximal cue assessment conditional on the goal, which is what a real
forager's nose does and what static curated scent cannot do.

It is deliberately **not** a second entry search. Measurement (§5.1)
showed that fusing a dense ranker into an already-correct lexical one
degrades it. The frontier has no such ranker to degrade.

### K.1 Contract

When the Gauntlet is **active** for a call, the candidate list of `look`
(`edges_out`/`edges_in`), `move` (`neighbors`) and `scan` (`nodes`) is
ordered by a blend of query proximity and the existing signal, **before**
the edge cap and the token budget are applied. Ordering changes; shapes,
budgets, truncation semantics and every other field do not.

**Availability is not consent.** The vector layer has two possible
consumers and the measurement above says opposite things about them, so
*having* an index MUST NOT decide *using* it for either:

| Consumer | Default | Why |
|---|---|---|
| entry search (`locate` under RRF) | **off** | fusing into an already-correct BM25 degrades it |
| the Gauntlet (frontier order) | **on** when ready | there is no query-dependent ranker there to degrade |

An implementation MUST therefore keep the layer's *readiness* separate from
each consumer's decision. Binding an embedding model to a forest turns on
the Gauntlet and MUST NOT turn on hybrid entry search: an operator who
picks up the instrument has not asked for the degradation, and a feature
that silently enables a measured regression is a trap, not a default.

The Gauntlet is active only when all of the following hold:

1. an embedder is configured, and
2. a Canopy index exists, is non-empty, and its recorded model matches the
   embedder's (K.4), and
3. a **goal vector** is available for the session (K.2), and
4. the call did not opt out (K.3).

If any fails, the primitive MUST behave exactly as it does without the
Gauntlet the same order, the same fields, the same bytes. Absence is not
a degraded mode; it is the Phase 0 contract, unchanged.

### K.2 The goal, and why it costs nothing

The goal vector is the embedding of the most recent `locate`/`harvest`
query in the session: the forager picks the instrument up when the hunt
starts and carries it for every hop after. `locate` MUST embed the query
whenever the layer is ready **for the goal**, whether or not it also
fuses the result into its own ranking. That is one embedding per hunt, not
per hop, and it is the entire running cost.

That cost runs inside whichever traced primitive needed the vector —
`locate` at the entry, a hop's `look`/`move` when the goal embeds lazily —
and is therefore named there: the primitive's Part D event carries it as
`embed_ms` (v0.68), so the one network round trip on the read path can
never be read as the forest's own work.

The separation matters for exactly the reason K.1 gives: the query is
embedded so the forager can *navigate* with it, not so entry search can
re-rank with it. Each subsequent hop is a dot
product over vectors already stored in the Canopy no network call, no
model call, and no tokens in either direction.

A caller MAY override the goal per call with an explicit `toward` string;
the implicit goal is what makes the feature free, and the explicit one is
what makes it testable.

**The read path embeds the query and nothing else (normative, v0.42).**
`locate`, `harvest` and the Gauntlet's goal MUST NOT embed *nodes*.
Refreshing stale vectors inside a read was one caller paying an ingest's
bill: the work is proportional to what somebody else wrote, it is
unbounded, and it lands on whoever asks next inside the primitive with
the tightest budget in the document (F.6). Re-embedding is maintenance
(J.13.4), triggered and observable, exactly as the catalog rebuild is
(J.13.3).

The cost of that separation is stated plainly rather than hidden: until a
refresh runs, a newly written node is **absent from the dense half** of
hybrid ranking. It is not absent from the forest the catalog upsert is
synchronous, so BM25 finds it on the next call, and every structural
primitive already does. The debt is reported (K.4) so it can be chosen,
which is the whole difference between a trade-off and a surprise.

The goal is session state and MUST be observable, never silent: a response
whose order was conditioned MUST say so the primitive reports that its
frontier was ranked and toward what. A reordering the reader cannot see is
a reordering the reader cannot audit, which is the same objection this
specification raises to every other invisible transformation.

### K.3 Opt-out, and the experiment it enables

Every affected primitive accepts an optional boolean that disables the
Gauntlet for that call. This is not a convenience: a feature that claims a
navigation gain MUST be measurable **against itself on the same corpus in
the same session**, and that requires turning it off without restarting
anything or rebuilding an index.

Consoles that expose navigation (the Playground) and the answering
composite (`answer`) MUST surface that switch, so an operator can compare
the two orders on their own corpus rather than trusting a table measured on
somebody else's.

**The entry-search switch is a different switch.** `answer` composes
`harvest`, which is `locate` + `sniff` and never hops, so a *Gauntlet*
control on an answering console would change nothing and a control that
changes nothing is worse than no control. What does change an answer is
K.1's other consumer: whether the vector layer is fused into entry search.
Calls that perform entry search (`locate`, `harvest`, `answer`) MUST
therefore accept an optional `hybrid` boolean, **defaulting to false on
every call**, for the same reason the opt-out exists: the published
degradation (R@1 1.00 → 0.40) has to be reproducible on the operator's own
corpus. It MUST NOT be sticky a request that omits it is a BM25 request,
whatever the previous request asked for.

*Deployment note (informative):* whether the Gauntlet is available at all
is a property of the forest's configuration, not of the caller's identity.
A deployment MAY additionally pin it on or off for a given credential, but
the default is per-forest availability plus per-call choice.

**Every surface, and the reply says whether it happened (v0.82).** The
rule above names the calls, and the MCP tools for two of them carried no
such parameter: the tool IS the call, and a menu that does not name a
parameter is v0.79's failure — for an agent the parameter does not exist.
And a call that asked for the layer on a forest without one was answered by
BM25 in silence, which is the lie C.13 forbids a filter to tell. Normative:

1. The `locate`, `harvest` and `answer` tools carry `hybrid`, forwarded
   exactly as REST forwards it (a host field, popped before the C.12
   table looks; declared in the table so the two surfaces are compared).
2. A response to a call that asked `hybrid: true` carries `hybrid: true |
   false` — whether the vector layer took part — and, when false,
   `hybrid_reason` naming K.4's state (`no-embedder`, `no-index`,
   `model-mismatch`). A call that did not ask carries neither field,
   byte-identical to before. The echo is read on the lane beside the
   switch and attached per serve, after the J.10.7 deposit, so a stored
   answer never freezes a layer's state and a hit says what is true today.
3. `forests()` and `/v1/forests` carry `hybrid: true | false` per forest —
   the deployment's shape, read before the first call, in J.10.11's sense.
   It is read off the `embed` binding and the index manifest and never by
   opening the forest: the listing is what every session starts with, and
   a listing touches no lane.

**F.212 (acceptance).** The three tools publish `hybrid`. On a forest with
no embedder bound, `answer(hybrid: true)` over MCP and over REST answers the
reply itself with `hybrid: false` and `hybrid_reason: "no-embedder"`; the
same call without the parameter carries neither field; `harvest` and
`locate` say the same; `forests()` and `/v1/forests` report `hybrid:
false`. On a forest with a canopy index built for the bound embedder the
same call carries `hybrid: true` and no reason, a store hit still says so,
and the listings report `hybrid: true`. Covered by tests.

### K.4 Index integrity (the mismatch guard)

The Canopy records the model that built it. Comparing a query embedded by
one model against vectors produced by another compares two unrelated
spaces: the result is not worse ranking, it is meaningless ranking, and it
fails silently because a dot product always returns a number.

Therefore: when the embedder's model differs from the index's recorded
model, the dense layer MUST be treated as **absent** hybrid `locate` off,
Gauntlet off, Phase 0 behaviour and the mismatch MUST be reported by the
forest's validation and by any surface that shows index status. Rebuilding
is the only resolution; a partial re-embed would leave the index in two
spaces at once.

**Status reports the debt (normative, v0.42).** The status surface of this
section MUST also carry `stale`: the number of nodes written since the
last build or refresh, and therefore absent from the dense half. It is
the number that predicts what a refresh costs and the only way an
operator can decide when to pay it; a layer that is quietly behind is
indistinguishable from one that is current.

### K.6 The embedding memo (v0.42)

`embed(model, text)` is a pure function of its inputs, so a Vine MAY
memoize it in the derived layer under exactly the C.6b.1 discipline:

- **Keyed by the model and the normalized text**, because a vector from
  one model in another model's space is the meaningless comparison K.4
  exists to prevent.
- **Only texts a caller supplies** queries, `toward` goals. A node's
  vector already has a home, the Canopy index itself, and storing it
  twice would make two answers to "what is this node's vector".
- **Disposable and bounded.** It lives in `_derived/`, may be dropped at
  any moment with no effect but latency, and MAY be evicted
  least-recently-used (H.6 is the precedent).
- **Never a substitute for the index.** A memo hit skips a round trip;
  it never makes an absent or mismatched index look present (K.4 stands
  ahead of it).

### K.5 Out of scope

Re-ranking node *bodies* (that is `sniff`'s job and it is literal by
contract); replacing heat with proximity (they answer different questions
and H's pheromone economics depend on heat remaining a memory); and any
behaviour that makes navigation *require* an embedder.

## Part L Extensions (third-party modules, v0.80)

### L.0 Why an extension is not a fork

Part G opens its extensibility section with a sentence that has held since
v0.9: "UIs and bots are MCP/library clients, not plugins." That sentence
drew the line in the right place and left a class of work with nowhere to
stand — the work that is neither a client nor a change to the contract, but
a **capability the deployment does not have**: transcribing an audio file,
converting a format nobody here has heard of, reading a proprietary export,
describing an image with a model this project never integrated.

Every one of those arrives with a dependency, and the dependency is the
whole problem. FFmpeg is GPL or LGPL depending on how it was built; a
document converter drags a machine-learning stack; a transcriber drags
another. `LICENSING.md` splits this tree Apache-2.0 (engine) / AGPL-3.0-only
(host), and that split holds only while the dependency list stays clean.
Pinning any of them makes this project their distributor.

An extension moves the decision to the operator, and the direction of that
move is the entire point. **This project MUST NOT distribute an extension's
bytes** — the curated index of L.2 carries signed *pointers*, never
artifacts. What is installed on an operator's machine is the operator's act,
under the extension's own licence, which MUST be shown before the install
completes.

The shape is a browser extension written in Python: one package carrying its
backend module *and* its console surface, declaring what it contributes,
installed and removed by the operator. It contributes at named seams; it
does not patch. That distinction is what leaves this project free to
refactor: an extension is coupled to a seam's published contract, never to
the shape of the code behind it.

### L.1 The package

An extension is a directory (delivered as a zip, or as a git tree — L.2)
whose root MUST carry `manifest.json` and MUST carry the module its manifest
names. Everything else is optional.

```
manifest.json         # identity, compat, permissions, contributions, config schema
main.py               # register(api) — the one activation entry point
worker.py             # functions declared heavy (L.5)
ui/panel.json         # declarative console contributions (L.11)
requirements.txt      # resolved into the extension's own environment
LICENSE               # the extension's own licence
```

The manifest MUST carry `id`, `version`, `station_compat`, `license` and
`contributes`. `id` MUST be unique within a deployment and is the namespace
for everything the extension creates (L.4 rule 5).

```json
{
  "id": "whisper",
  "version": "1.2.0",
  "station_compat": ">=0.80,<0.90",
  "license": "MIT",
  "permissions": {
    "network": ["api.openai.com"],
    "filesystem": "none",
    "capabilities": ["ingest"]
  },
  "models": {
    "requires": [],
    "registers": [{ "role": "transcribe", "kind": "transcribe",
                    "description": "Turns a recording into text." }]
  },
  "contributes": {
    "converters": [
      { "extensions": [".mp3", ".m4a", ".wav"],
        "handler": "worker:transcribe", "heavy": true }
    ],
    "tools": [{ "name": "transcribe", "handler": "main:tool_transcribe" }],
    "panel": "ui/panel.json"
  },
  "config": {
    "language": { "type": "string", "default": "auto" },
    "api_key":  { "type": "string", "secret": true }
  }
}
```

**`station_compat` is a range against the host's published version** — the
same string `forests()` already serves (J.1.2 rule 6). An install whose
range excludes the running host MUST be refused by name and version, never
attempted; a host upgrade that falls outside an installed extension's range
MUST disable it and say so, never load it and hope.

**What the host's version promises, and what it does not.** The minor is
the spec version a release implements, so `0.81.x` implements this
document; the patch is every release that cuts no spec. While the major is
`0` a **patch may change behaviour**, and this specification says so rather
than letting an author infer a guarantee from the shape of a number. An
extension SHOULD therefore pin to the minor it was written and tested
against (`>=0.81,<0.82`). A wider range is legal and means exactly what it
says — *I accept whatever the next minor does to me* — which is a
reasonable choice for a small surface and an unreasonable one for anything
that reads a seam closely. The authoring reference (L.16) MUST state this
where the range is copied from, because the person copying it is the person
who has no other source.

### L.2 Sources, resolution and trust

An extension MAY arrive from four places, and they MUST all pass through one
resolver:

| Source | Form |
|---|---|
| curated index | `vine ext install whisper` |
| git | `vine ext install github.com/org/monkeyllm-whisper@v1.2.0` |
| release archive | `vine ext install https://.../whisper-1.2.0.zip` |
| local file | `vine ext install ./whisper-1.2.0.zip` |
| uploaded archive | the operator's own bytes, from a browser (v0.81) |

**The uploaded archive is the door the others do not open.** "A local file"
is a path on the **host**, which through a browser is the container's
filesystem — so an operator holding an extension they just wrote had no
route to a remote Station short of publishing it to git, and the local-file
door served only somebody with a shell there, who would have used the CLI.
Bytes arrive as `{name, b64}`, the shape J.8 has carried since v0.48, and
are written into the workdir as the archive L.2 already resolves: a fifth
door, not a fifth resolver.

Two rules ride with it. It is **`unverified` by construction** — an upload
carries no forge and no index identity, so there is nothing that could be
verified and the tier MUST say so rather than implying a check happened.
And it is **bounded** (`MONKEYLLM_STATION_EXT_UPLOAD_MAX_MB`, 25 by
default), because this door is for an extension's own code: dependencies
are resolved at install (L.5), and a vendored-wheel bundle belongs to the
local-file route, where the bytes are already on the host.

**Rule 1 — the source resolves to an immutable artifact before anything is
validated.** A git ref MUST be resolved to a commit SHA, and the **SHA** is
what the install record holds. A tag can be force-pushed and a branch moves;
"the thing that was signed" MUST be the thing that runs. `@v1.2.0` means *the
SHA that tag pointed at when this operator installed*.

**Rule 2 — a moving ref is allowed and marked.** `@main` MAY be installed:
an author developing an extension must not have to cut a release per test.
The record MUST carry `tracking: <ref>` beside the SHA, and every surface
naming the extension MUST name the ref beside it — "the same extension" on
two deployments is otherwise not the same code. Being *behind* costs a
network round trip, so it MUST be reported on demand (`vine ext outdated`)
and MUST NOT be computed by a listing, which MUST stay an offline call.

**Rule 3 — three trust tiers, recorded and shown.**

| Tier | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `verified` | id from the curated index; the index carries the expected signing identity and the artifact matches it |
| `signed` | git source at a **signed tag**, verified against the public keys the forge publishes for the author's account |
| `unverified` | everything else — unsigned tags, tracked branches, plain archives, local files |

Two consequences follow rather than being decided: a **tracked branch is
`unverified` by construction** (a branch carries no tag, so there is nothing
to verify), and **`signed` requires the network at install time**, because
the keys live at the forge — an air-gapped deployment installing from a
local file reaches `unverified` or `verified`, never `signed`.

The tier MUST appear everywhere the extension appears. An extension MUST NOT
change tier quietly: a source that was `signed` and comes back unsigned MUST
refuse the update until the operator acknowledges it.

**Rule 4 — the verifying identity is recorded.** Delegating identity to the
forge is what avoids running a key infrastructure, and its cost is stated
rather than hidden: **a compromised forge account is a compromised
extension.** The install record MUST hold the account and the key
fingerprint that verified it, and a change on update MUST be surfaced, not
accepted silently. Repo transfers and key rotations become visible without
anybody maintaining a keyring.

**Rule 5 — what validation cannot promise.** Resolving `requirements.txt`
executes third-party build code by construction — that is true of pip
everywhere — and a git source additionally runs the author's build backend.
The conformance kit (L.9 rule 1) therefore does **not** run before
third-party code runs; it runs before anything is **registered**. The
documentation MUST say this in those words, because it is the reason the
signature tier carries more weight than the kit does.

### L.3 The seam catalogue and precedence

An extension **claims** a seam; it MUST NOT patch, wrap or replace anything
this specification did not name. A seam absent from this catalogue is not an
extension point, and reaching one is a defect regardless of whether it
works.

| Seam | Contributes | Precedence |
|---|---|---|
| `converters` | a file extension → a document (G.2) | operator command hooks > extensions by install order > entry points > built-ins |
| `curation` | an `on_curate` hook (G.4) | all hooks run, in install order |
| `events` | a handler for `plant`/`graft`/`prune`/`ingest`/`answer` | all handlers run, order unspecified |
| `jobs` | maintenance beside the Ranger (H), **pulled** not scheduled | independent |
| `tools` | an MCP tool (C, J.1) | namespaced; collision refuses the install |
| `routes` | a REST route under `/v1/ext/<id>/` (J) | namespaced by the path, so a contribution can never take a name the product needs |
| `panel` | a console contribution (L.11) | one per extension |
| `ranking` | an ordering contribution to `locate`/`harvest` | first claimant wins |
| `prompt` | a contribution to the `answer` prompt (J.10) | first claimant wins |
| `roles` | a model role and its `kind` (L.6) | collision refuses the install |

`discover_converters` (G.2) already works this way — config command hooks >
injected extras > entry points > built-ins — so the model is not new. It is
the existing one, published with a version.

**Every seam DECLARES its handler's contract (v0.81).** What a `curation`
handler receives, what an `events` handler receives and what each must hand
back were prose here and nowhere in the code, so the conformance kit could
answer "it works" about an extension whose handler took the wrong
parameters — and the author learned otherwise on the first ingest, at
whatever hour that ran. The declaration lives beside the seam catalogue,
the kit checks a handler's signature against it **at install** (L.9 rule
1), and the authoring reference (L.16) is generated from the same
declaration rather than transcribed beside it.

The rule is about **defaults**, not about `**kwargs`. A handler MAY omit
any parameter it does not use; a parameter the seam does not pass is fine
when it carries a **default** (it simply keeps it) and is a fault when it
does not, whatever else the signature accepts.

`**kwargs` excuses nothing, and the first draft of this paragraph said it
did — wrongly, in the exact case it was written for. Given `def
on_event(event, forrest, **rest)` the host passes `forest`, `**rest`
absorbs it, and `forrest` is still unfilled: a `TypeError` at call time,
which for a `curation` handler is whatever hour the next ingest runs. That
is the silence this check exists to break, so the check may not be excused
by the construct that hides it.

The check MUST read the author's **source** rather than import it: a
`heavy` handler's module imports the very dependency L.5 keeps out of this
process, so a check that imported would break the rule that protects the
deployment in order to catch a typo — and it would run third-party code at
kit time, which L.2 rule 5 is careful to say the kit does not do.

**The last two seams carry a rule the others do not.** A `ranking` or
`prompt` contribution changes what the product answers, and an operator
comparing a bad answer against a good one has no way to know an extension is
between them. Both MUST therefore be **named in the Part D trace** of every
call they touch, and the trace's consumers (J.10.4 `explain`, J.5.15, the
Ask console) MUST render that name. A contribution that cannot be attributed
MUST NOT be admitted.

Each of them is also bounded by what it may not do:

- A **`ranking`** contribution may reorder and drop; it MUST NOT invent. A
  result it returns that was not handed to it MUST be discarded — G.4.2.1's
  rule about hallucinated targets, applied to ordering. It runs **before**
  the budget, so what it promoted is what survives the cut rather than being
  reordered inside a set somebody else already chose.
- A **`prompt`** contribution is **appended**, never substituted. The rules
  the product's own answers depend on — citation, the refusal to invent, the
  stated budget — MUST NOT be removable by an extension.
- Either one raising leaves the call exactly as it would have been without
  it (L.7 rule 5), which for `ranking` is the original order and for
  `prompt` is the unmodified system message.

### L.4 `register(api)`

An extension is activated by exactly one call, `register(api)`, in the module
its manifest names. It MUST NOT act at import time.

`api` is **enumerated**: it exposes what this specification lists and
nothing more, and a new engine capability requires its own line here before
an extension can reach it. That is the same construction `ScopedVine` uses,
for the same reason — a surface that forwards whatever it is given is not a
surface, it is an accident.

1. **`api.contribute(seam, handler, **spec)`** — the only way to claim a
   seam. Claims made outside `register` MUST be refused.
2. **`api.config`** — the extension's own settings, validated against the
   manifest's `config` block. A field declared `secret: true` is readable
   here and MUST NOT be readable anywhere the extension can export it (L.7
   rule 4).
3. **`api.models.complete(role=..., ...)`** and
   **`api.models.transcribe(role=..., audio=...)`** — L.6. The extension MUST
   NOT receive an endpoint, a key, or `has_key`. Two methods rather than one
   because they are two APIs: a chat turn is a JSON body to
   `/chat/completions` and a transcription is a multipart upload to a
   different path. Collapsing them would put the difference in a caller's
   arguments, where the binding cannot see it — which is the whole reason a
   role carries a `kind`.
4. **`api.vine`** — a `ScopedVine` carrying **the caller's** scope, never a
   raw `Vine` and never a widened one. Every J.3 guarantee survives an
   extension unchanged: an extension tool asked for an out-of-scope id MUST
   return the byte-identical `E_NOT_FOUND` a primitive returns.
5. **`api.namespace`** — every id, tool name, route and table the extension
   creates MUST begin with it. A tool named outside the namespace MUST
   refuse the install rather than be renamed silently.
6. **`api.log`** — the host's own log, tagged with the extension id.

An extension's module MUST be executed **once per load**. A loader touches
it at least twice — for `register` and again for each declared handler — and
executing it twice gives the extension two module objects: `register()`
writes to one and its handlers read from the other, so any module-level
state the author keeps (a client, a cache, a counter) silently splits in
half. Nothing raises, which is exactly why the rule is written down.

Where a process legitimately holds two installs of one `id` — a test that
builds several hosts, a staging copy beside a live one — they MUST be
distinct modules. The identity of a loaded module is therefore the installed
**tree**, never the `id` alone.

### L.5 The worker

The manifest MAY mark a handler `heavy: true`. A heavy handler MUST run in
the extension's own environment, in a separate process, and MUST NOT be
imported into the host's interpreter.

This is what keeps the dependency that motivated the extension out of the
process that serves the forest: a transcriber's machine-learning stack, a
converter's document toolchain, a binary that is not Python at all. The host
MUST enforce a wall-clock timeout and MUST treat a worker's death as a
handler failure (L.7 rule 5), never as a host failure.

The worker protocol MUST be language-neutral in shape — a request and a
response over a pipe, values that survive JSON — so that a future
non-Python worker is a packaging question and not a contract change. This
version ships one SDK.

**The request carries the extension's resolved config (v0.84).** A heavy
handler received its arguments and nothing else, so an extension whose
work has knobs had nowhere to read them from: the first converter written
against this protocol declares an empty `config` block and documents every
one of its settings as an **environment variable** instead, in its own
source, as the honest description of what the transport could carry — and
the list has grown with each of its versions. That defeats L.10's rule
from the other side — the config schema is the source of truth, and a
setting the schema cannot express is a setting no console and no `vine ext
config` can reach — and it makes a per-deployment knob out of something
that should be a per-install one.

The worker request MUST therefore carry the extension's **resolved**
config — the manifest's declared defaults (L.10) overlaid with the
operator's stored values, resolved by the host at call time so an edit
takes effect without a restart (L.7 rule 4's live read) — beside the
handler's arguments.

Two rules keep it compatible and honest:

1. **A handler that does not ask never sees it.** The value is passed only
   to a handler that declares a `config` parameter, which the L.9 contract
   check already knows how to see (it reads the author's source and never
   imports it). A v0.83 worker declaring `convert(path)` receives exactly
   what it receives today, byte for byte.
2. **A declared secret travels like every other credential**: to the
   worker, which is the process that needs it, and never to a log, a
   report, an audit row or a crash trace. The worker protocol stays
   language-neutral in shape — one JSON request in, one JSON response out
   — so a non-Python worker reads `config` out of the request like any
   other field.

### L.6 Models: roles, never keys (amends J.10)

An extension MAY **require** roles the deployment already binds, and MAY
**register** a role of its own.

- **A registered role appears wherever bound roles appear** and is bound by
  the operator to a provider they already pay for. The extension therefore
  needs no key of its own, and the deployment keeps one place where model
  spend is configured.

  **Rule 1 (v0.83): appearing means bindable, on every surface.** The
  bind route MUST accept every role a loaded extension registers, and the
  read beside it (`GET /v1/admin/models`) MUST carry `roles`: every
  bindable role with its `kind`, whether it is the product's own
  (`builtin`) or an extension's (`ext`), and its `description` — the
  manifest's for a registered role (L.1). A console MUST render its role
  cards from that list and MUST NOT keep one of its own, and MUST shape
  the binding form by `kind`: a `transcribe` binding has no reply length
  and no reasoning switch, because the call is a multipart upload and not
  a chat turn. The v0.82 Station registered the role, listed it on the
  Extensions console, and refused to bind it on the Models console and on
  the route alike — the sentence above was true of the list and false of
  the act.
- **A role carries a `kind`** — `chat`, `embed`, `vision`, `transcribe`,
  `rerank` — because transcription is not `/chat/completions`. Without
  `kind` an entire class of extension has nowhere to bind, and the binding
  UI cannot know what to ask for.
- **A required role with no binding MUST refuse the install**, by name, at
  install time. Discovering it at the first transcription is discovering it
  in front of a user.
- **The extension MUST NOT receive credentials.** `api.models` hands it a
  bound caller; the endpoint and the key stay under J.10.2's custody
  exactly as they do for every other consumer.
- **Every extension model call MUST be metered** and MUST reach the J.4.2
  row with its `usd`/`tokens`/`model_ms`. Unmetered extension spend is a
  bill with nobody's name on it, which is the failure J.4.2 was written
  against.

### L.7 Authority, audit and quota (amends J.4.2)

1. **The owner installs; a forest's admin enables.** Installation puts
   third-party code in the host's process and therefore within reach of
   every forest, so it MUST require the authority that covers every forest
   (J.10.2's reach rule). Enablement decides what acts on one forest's
   material and MUST require that forest's `admin`. An admin MUST NOT be
   able to install: a local decision with a global effect is not a local
   decision.
2. **Enabled on a forest means published on that forest.** An extension's
   tools and routes MUST be visible exactly where it is enabled; a key
   reaching several forests sees the union. There is no second opt-in
   control, and there MUST NOT be one — J.1.2 rule 4 already says a surface
   with nothing behind it is not announced.

   MCP's `tools/list` is per **connection** while enablement is per
   **forest**, so the menu a key is served MUST be the union of the
   extensions enabled on the forests **that key reaches**. Two consequences
   are intended rather than tolerated: two keys on one deployment can be
   served different menus, and an extension enabled nowhere the key reaches
   is **invisible** rather than merely refusing — a tool that can only ever
   refuse costs every session its description and teaches nothing.

   The per-call check is a **separate** decision and is the real gate:
   listing answers *what is worth showing*, calling answers *what is
   allowed*. A tool called on a forest that has not enabled its extension
   MUST answer the byte-identical `E_NOT_FOUND` an unknown tool answers —
   J.3's oracle does not acquire an exception because the caller guessed a
   name. And because the filter decides what a key is shown, an
   implementation that cannot apply it MUST withhold every extension tool
   and say so: fewer tools than the rule allows is a degradation, more is a
   disclosure.
3. **The audit row keeps the human and names the extension.** J.4.2's row
   gains **`via`** (`ext:<id>`), nullable, emitted only when an extension
   was in the path. `principal` MUST remain whoever caused the act — a
   forensic question is *who asked for this*, and an extension is not an
   answer to it. A row written before this version reads `via` as
   **absent**, never as "no extension", which is J.4.2's own rule about
   fields that lie by omission.
4. **Config is stored under the host's custody, and a secret never leaves
   it.** A field declared `secret: true` MUST NOT be returned by any read
   surface (`has_value` is the answer), MUST NOT be written to a versioned
   file, and MUST NOT be included in a webhook payload, an export, a
   snapshot or a log line. On a host with no registry (L.12) a declared
   secret MUST come from the environment and the loader MUST refuse a
   versioned config file that carries one.
5. **A raising extension is contained.** A failure inside a seam MUST fall
   back to the behaviour that would have applied without the extension —
   the built-in converter, the unmodified ordering, the absent hook — and
   MUST be reported (the ingest report, the trace, the log). This is G.5.1's
   rule for a describer that raises, generalised: an extension may fail to
   help, and may not fail the act.
6. **Quota is per extension per forest, and exhaustion is a refusal.** The
   operator MAY set a ceiling on an extension's model spend; reaching it
   MUST refuse in the envelope shape (`E_EXT_QUOTA`) and MUST be audited.
   Silence at the ceiling would be a stop nobody could distinguish from a
   bug.

### L.8 Lifecycle

Install → restart → enable per forest → run → disable → uninstall →
restart.

**The restart is required and MUST be stated.** Python does not unload a
module, so "disabled" without a restart means the code is still resident.
The host MUST NOT imply an unload that did not happen; a console MUST say
"disabled; memory released at the next restart". On a CLI host the
requirement costs nothing — every invocation is already a fresh process.

**A first install MAY be active at once (v0.83).** The restart is about
*unloading*. An `id` this process has never loaded has nothing to unload,
so a host MAY activate it in the running registry the moment the install
record is written, through the same loader and the same per-forest
enablement every other extension goes through. The install response MUST
say which happened — `activated: true` with `restart_required: false`, or
the reverse — and the listing MUST carry `loaded` per extension, so an
operator can tell "installed" from "installed and serving". Reinstalling,
updating or removing an id that IS loaded keeps the restart, because that
is the case Python cannot honour. An activation that fails MUST NOT fail
the install: the record stands, `restart_required` is `true`, and the
failure is named.

**Uninstall touches nothing in a forest.** Nodes stay, the git history stays,
the passports stay. But a `type` or `rel` the extension declared in a
forest's dialect (A.2) stops being declared, and A.2 then refuses the next
write that uses it. The host MUST therefore **name what will start being
refused** — every token the extension declared that no other extension
declares — before the operator confirms.

**Config is quarantined, not deleted.** A failed upgrade must be
recoverable, so config survives uninstall marked orphaned and is recovered
by reinstalling the same `id`. Quarantined secrets MUST expire and MUST be
listed somewhere an operator can see them: a secret that outlives its
extension and is visible to nobody is the worst of both choices.

### L.9 The four controls

Each does a different job, and conflating them is how a deployment comes to
believe it is protected by the one that does not protect it.

1. **Conformance kit** — the manifest against the schema, `station_compat`
   against the host, declared handlers importable **and matching their
   seam's declared contract (L.3, v0.81)**, a document round-trip against
   the fixture forest, and L.10's configurability rule. This is a
   **compatibility** control. The documentation MUST say plainly that it is
   not a security control: it establishes that an extension works, never
   that it is honest.
2. **Declared permissions** — network hosts, filesystem, capabilities,
   granted item by item at install. In the host's own process these
   **inform**; only what runs in a worker (L.5) can be **contained**. An
   install screen MUST NOT imply otherwise.
3. **Signature and the curated index** — L.2 rules 3 and 4.
4. **Operator sovereignty** — the licence, the permissions, the source and
   the tier are shown, and the operator decides. Nothing installs
   unattended.

### L.10 A contribution the host cannot serve

A CLI host has no console, so a declared panel has nowhere to draw. The rule
is J.1.2 rule 4 applied to extensions: **a contribution the host cannot
serve is inert and named, never an error.**

- The loader MUST parse and validate every contribution, including those it
  cannot serve, so a broken panel is caught on the author's machine instead
  of in a Station.
- It MUST NOT render it; it exposes the parsed contribution and a host that
  has that surface draws it.
- A listing MUST say so — `panel: declared (no host surface)`.

The half that matters more is configuration. **The config schema is the
source of truth and a panel is decoration over it.** A console renders a
form from the manifest's `config` block; a CLI reads the same block to set
and validate the same values. A registered role binds through the models
console on one host and through the environment on the other — one role, two
binding surfaces.

The conformance kit MUST enforce it: **an extension with a required setting
that has no entry in the config schema fails.** That single rule is what
keeps a console-less host first-class rather than degraded.

A panel-only extension is legitimate and simply does nothing where there is
no console. The listing says so rather than implying it is running.

### L.11 The console surface (amends J.5)

An extension's console contribution is **declarative**: the manifest
describes panels, fields, tables and actions, and the console renders them
with its own components.

This is not a stylistic preference. J.5.13 admits script only by hash
computed from the built shell, with no `unsafe-eval` and `connect-src
'self'`; a third-party script inside the console's origin would run with the
operator's session against every forest they can reach, which is the
vulnerability class this rule exists to prevent. **The console MUST NOT
execute extension-supplied script in its own origin**, and MUST NOT relax
its CSP to admit one.

A vocabulary this specification has not named cannot be drawn. That is the
accepted cost, and it is bounded: the vocabulary grows by amendment, and an
extension needing more than it offers still has its REST route and the
operator's browser.

**The install is one legible act (v0.83).** The console that installs an
extension is used by the person least able to read a mechanism, so the
shape of the act is normative:

1. **The primary action sits beside the thing it acts on**, and it is the
   only primary control on the card. A file chosen at the bottom of a card
   and a button at its top right are two places for one act, and the
   v0.82 console shipped exactly that: an operator chose a zip, saw the
   distant button change shade, and did not read it as the next step.
2. **Choosing is not an act; reviewing is.** Typing a source or choosing a
   file changes nothing on the host. The review (L.9 rule 4) is the first
   call, and its result — licence, source, tier, permissions, what it
   contributes, what it registers — MUST be shown **in place**, under the
   choice that produced it, with the install control beside it. A dialog
   that opens over the card is a third place.
3. **Enabling MAY ride the install.** Installing from a forest's console
   MAY enable the extension on that forest in the same act, when the
   principal administers it, through a visible control that defaults ON —
   installing from a forest is a statement of intent about that forest.
   The route takes `enable_on: <forest>`, applies it after the record is
   written, by the enablement path L.7 rule 2 already governs, and never
   for a forest the principal does not administer.
4. **The outcome says what to do next.** After the install the console
   MUST state, in this order: whether the extension is active now or
   after a restart (L.8); what it now accepts (formats, from J.8.5) and
   what it now offers (roles, tools); and what is still missing before it
   can be used — a role to bind, named, with the way to the console that
   binds it. An install that ends in a green tick and no sentence is the
   install the operator reported.

### L.12 Where the mechanism lives

Part J calls the Station a *privileged client* of the engine — "the engine
gains nothing, loses nothing". Extensions are not the exception. **The
mechanism is the engine's; the governance is the Station's**, which is the
cut that already separates `Vine` from `ScopedVine`.

| Engine | Station |
|---|---|
| manifest schema, source resolver, tiers, signature | owner/admin authority (L.7 rule 1) |
| conformance kit | secret custody (L.7 rule 4) |
| environment resolution, loader, `register(api)` | per-forest quota (L.7 rule 6) |
| seam precedence, worker protocol | `via` in the audit row (L.7 rule 3) |
| the CLI: install, update, list, config, enable, remove | the console (L.11), the curated index |

It follows that **an operator with no Station installs extensions**, and
that is required, not incidental: the engine is the artifact that spreads,
and a capability reachable only through the AGPL host would make every
extension author a client of that host.

Two rules make it work:

- **Global install is a host-level directory; per-forest enablement is a
  line in the forest's `_meta/`.** Enablement is therefore versioned and
  travels in a snapshot (Part I), so a forest carries **which extensions it
  expects**. `validate` MUST report an expected-but-absent extension —
  otherwise an `.mp3` is converted by the built-in stub and nobody is told.
  Installation state MUST NOT live in `_derived/`, which is disposable and
  which `reindex` may delete.

  Writing that line MUST also **commit** it. A snapshot is a git bundle, so
  a file merely sitting in a versioned directory travels in nothing, and
  "it is versioned" would be true of the path and false of the artifact.
  A.3.1's guard on the ordinary commit path — only `.md` is staged, so
  binaries cannot enter forest git — is NOT relaxed for this: the write
  goes through a second, narrower door that admits `.yaml` and `.md`
  **under `_meta/` only**. A guard widened for a convenience is a guard
  that has stopped meaning anything, and the capability this needs is small
  enough to be named rather than implied.
- **`_meta` declares expectation and never grants it.** A forest that
  expects an extension the deployment has not installed MUST appear in the
  health report; it MUST NOT cause an install.

The loader MUST be optional (`monkeyllm[extensions]`). Absent, the base
install MUST load with the loader inert — never an import error — because
an embedder of the engine did not ask for environment management.

### L.13 Boundaries that stay closed

Unchanged, and an extension reaching any of them is a defect:

- Primitive semantics, token budgets and truncation contracts.
- The `locate`/`sniff` split; `tend` staying DML-only; `plant`'s declarative
  schema as the only path to a table.
- **J.3's oracle.** An extension tool MUST NOT disclose the existence of a
  node outside its caller's scope, by any channel including timing-free
  ones like a count or a distinct error.
- Binaries never entering forest git (A.3.1).
- A new node `type` or `rel` is declared in the forest's dialect (A.2),
  through the seam that already exists, never around it.

### L.14 Acceptance criteria

**F.174.** A manifest failing the schema, `station_compat`, or the
conformance kit installs **nothing**: no environment, no record, no
registration.

**F.175.** A heavy handler's dependency is absent from the host's own
interpreter — asserted by importing it in-process and expecting failure —
while the handler itself runs.

**F.176.** An extension requiring a role with no binding refuses the install
and names the role.

**F.177.** An extension model call reaches the J.4.2 row with the human
`principal`, `via: ext:<id>`, and its cost and `model_ms`.

**F.178.** Quota exhaustion refuses in the envelope shape, is audited, and
the following period admits again.

**F.179.** An extension tool asked for an out-of-scope id returns the
byte-identical `E_NOT_FOUND` a primitive returns.

**F.180.** Enabling on forest A publishes the tool to a key holding A and
not to a key holding only B; a key holding both is served the union, an
anonymous caller is served none, and calling the tool on B answers the
byte-identical `E_NOT_FOUND` an unknown tool answers.

**F.181.** Uninstall names every `type`/`rel` that will start being refused
before confirmation, and the forest's files are byte-identical afterwards.

**F.182.** Quarantined config is recovered by reinstalling the same `id`,
and expires on schedule.

**F.183.** An extension raising inside a seam is contained: ingest falls
back to the built-in converter, the batch completes, and the report names
the extension.

**F.184.** A `ranking` or `prompt` contribution is named in the Part D trace
and rendered by the trace's consumers.

**F.185.** An unsigned source installs only after an explicit
acknowledgement; the tier is recorded and shown, and a `signed` extension
returning unsigned refuses the update.

**F.186.** An extension installs and runs on an engine-only host with no
Station: install, enablement written to the forest's `_meta/`, and the
converter claiming its extension on the next ingest. The enablement is
**committed**, so a snapshot taken afterwards carries it; the ordinary
commit path still refuses a non-`.md` file.

**F.187.** `validate` names an extension a forest expects and that is not
installed; the base install without the optional extra loads with the loader
inert rather than raising.

**F.188.** A versioned config file carrying a field the manifest declared
`secret` is refused.

**F.189.** A git install records the resolved commit SHA rather than the
ref; the same `@tag` installed after the tag moved resolves to a different
SHA and the host says so.

**F.190.** An extension declaring a panel installs and runs on a
console-less host: the panel is validated, reported unserved, and nothing
errors.

**F.191.** Every required setting is reachable without a console, and the
kit fails an extension whose required setting has no schema entry.

**F.192.** A failed update leaves the previous install running and
unmodified.

**F.193.** An install from a branch records the SHA, is marked `tracking`,
lands in the `unverified` tier, and the listing names the ref while making
no network call.

**F.194.** A signed tag verifies against the forge's published keys and
reaches `signed`; the verifying identity is recorded, and an install whose
identity changed refuses the update until acknowledged.

**F.195.** An `events` contribution is called for an event on a forest that
enabled it and not for the same event on one that did not; a handler that
raises does not fail the act that emitted it.

**F.196.** A `routes` contribution answers under `/v1/ext/<id>/<name>`, is
audited with `via`, and answers the byte-identical `E_NOT_FOUND` for an
unknown name, an unreached forest, and a forest that has not enabled it.

**F.197.** A `jobs` contribution is listed and runnable on a forest that
enabled it and is absent on one that did not.

**F.198.** A `ranking` contribution reorders the sweep's results, cannot add
one that was not handed to it, and names itself on the Part D event; a
`prompt` contribution is appended to the system message and cannot remove
what was there.

**F.213 (v0.83).** `supported_formats` answers every extension the chain
claims in discovery order, naming the first claimant, and an extension
enabled on a forest appears in that forest's answer above the built-in for
the same extension while a command hook appears above both.

**F.214 (v0.83).** `GET /v1/forests/{f}/ingest` carries `formats`, and a
forest that enables a converter extension lists its extensions there while
a forest that does not enable it does not.

**F.215 (v0.83).** `GET /v1/admin/models` carries `roles` naming every
built-in role and every role a loaded extension registers, with `kind`,
origin and description; `POST` binds a registered role and refuses an
unknown name by listing what it would accept.

**F.216 (v0.83).** Installing an id not loaded in this process activates
it: the response says `activated: true`, the listing says `loaded: true`,
its roles are bindable and its formats are accepted without a restart;
reinstalling a loaded id answers `restart_required: true`.

**F.217 (v0.83).** `install` with `enable_on` enables the extension on that
forest in the same act for a principal who administers it, and refuses the
enablement — not the install — for one who does not.

**F.218 (v0.83).** The consoles carry no list of their own: the ingest
console's accepted formats, the Models console's role cards and the
Extensions console's install flow are read off the host's answers, asserted
statically on the source (F.137's boundary) with the previous console as
the negative control.

**F.228 (v0.84).** The worker knows its settings. A heavy handler
declaring `convert(path, config)` receives the manifest's defaults
overlaid with the operator's stored values, and a value changed through
the config surface reaches the NEXT call with no restart; a handler
declaring `convert(path)` is called exactly as in v0.83 and the extra
field changes nothing. A declared secret reaches the worker and appears in
no report, log, audit row or error, including the error raised when the
handler itself fails.

### L.16 The authoring surface (v0.81)

Part L shipped a mechanism and no way in. The only document that named
extensions described the world before them, nothing taught how to write
one, and the console offered an author no door. A contract nobody can find
the entrance to is a contract with one implementer.

**Rule 1 — prose is written, schemas are derived.** The text that teaches —
what a seam is, why an extension contributes instead of patching, a worked
example — is written by people and lives in the repository, where it is
read without running anything. The **schemas** MUST be generated from the
definitions themselves: the manifest's own JSON schema, the seam contracts
of L.3, the role `kind`s of L.6, the config field types. A transcribed
schema is a schema that lies the first time a seam is added, and it lies
silently, to exactly the person who has no other source.

**Rule 2 — the material states which host it came from.** An authoring
reference carries the host's version (J.1.2 rule 6's rule, applied to the
thing an author copies a `station_compat` range out of), so an example that
has aged says so instead of teaching a range that no longer fits.

**Rule 3 — writing is not installing.** The authoring surface MUST be
offered to anyone signed in, and MUST NOT be gated on the authority to
install. J.5.12 settled the same question for skills — "the person who may
read the forest is the person whose AI may learn to" — and it holds harder
here: an extension is written on a laptop and installed by whoever governs
the deployment, so gating the documentation on L.7 rule 1's authority
withholds it from the only person who needs it.

**Rule 4 — what it may not become.** The authoring surface is documentation
and a schema. It MUST NOT accept an extension, install one, execute one, or
carry a credential; and it MUST NOT be a second description of the manifest
that could disagree with the loader's.

**F.199.** An extension is installed from an **uploaded** archive with no
path on the host: the bytes arrive as `{name, b64}`, the tier is
`unverified`, and it installs only on an explicit acknowledgement.

**F.200.** An upload over the ceiling is refused **before** it is written,
naming the ceiling and the size; the refusal stages nothing.

**F.201.** An uploaded archive whose member escapes its root is refused as
a whole archive, never member-skipped.

**F.202.** A handler whose signature does not match its seam's declared
contract **fails the conformance kit**, naming the seam, the parameter and
what the seam passes — including when the handler also takes `**kwargs`,
which excuses nothing. A handler omitting a parameter it does not use
passes, and the check never imports the module it reads.

**F.203.** The authoring schema is **derived**: adding a seam to the
catalogue changes it with no second edit, and the served document names the
host's version.

**F.204.** The authoring surface is reachable by a signed-in principal who
may not install, and it offers no way to install, execute or upload.

**F.205.** Every seam in the catalogue has a declared contract, and every
declared contract belongs to a seam in the catalogue.

### L.15 Out of scope

A hosted marketplace with accounts or payments (the index is a signed file);
extensions in other languages (the worker protocol must not forbid one, but
this version ships one SDK); hot install or upgrade without a restart; any
relaxation of L.13.
